lines: Dry rows and trampled crops teach a farmer to watch every footstep.
The soil's been kind lately. That's more than I can say for some visitors.
Seeds are small, but they know how to make a person <pulse>wait</pulse>.
Good rain is a blessing. Too much rain is work wearing a blessing mask.
A harvest only comes together when every little job gets done.
Bread starts long before the oven. Most good things do.
Most days, I am at the fields, trying to keep rain and soil from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think farming is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it matters to everyone.
I trust a good hoe more than a loud promise. The hoe has less to prove.
Fields reward people who return even when yesterday was unkind.
A seed is a small promise that still expects real work.
Rain can save a field or ruin a morning. Sometimes it tries both.
You learn patience when the crops answer every question slowly.
A village eats because someone kept doing dull work carefully.
Good soil does not forgive boots as quickly as people do.
The rows look quiet, but they keep very strict accounts.
A harvest tells you who watched the weather and who only watched the basket.
Farming is long hours, a sore back, and hoping the weather behaves.
The sun gets credit for work it never finished alone.
Every loaf begins as somebody kneeling in the dirt.
Bad weather has a way of finding the loose fence first.
I trust steady hands more than lucky skies.
The field never cares how important anyone thinks they are.
Crops are patient, but hunger is not.
You remember that walk through {follow_biome}? I have tilled softer ground than that road.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My boots carried half of it home.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to pack as if supper might be late.
I kept judging the soil beside the road. It was easier than thinking about the distance.
The farther we went, the more I worried about who was tending the fields.
I counted meals instead of miles. The number was still too large.
You kept us moving when I would have stopped to rest.
I missed the smell of turned earth before the village was even out of sight.
That road taught me why a full water skin matters more than a light pack.
I remember finding seeds in my pocket and wondering if they would ever reach soil again.
My legs complained for two days after we came home.
The first fenced field on the return told me we were finally close.
I slept better in the barn that night than I had anywhere on the road.
Next time I will leave clearer instructions for the crops before going.
I learned that hard ground can tire you faster than honest fieldwork.
You found a safe place to stop before dark. I have not forgotten that.
Every loaf we carried felt more valuable by the end of the trip.
I was glad to hear village animals before I could see the roofs.
The journey made our muddy lanes look almost welcoming.
If I follow you again, I am bringing better boots and twice the bread.
Boats are not much like fields. No furrows, no rows, just water deciding if it likes you.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.
I did not know a boat could feel so small until the shore vanished.
The water was calm, which somehow made every strange sound worse.
I watched the horizon until my eyes hurt.
Next time I am bringing food that does not roll across the boat.
You made rowing look easier than it felt.
I kept one hand on the boat and the other on my courage.
Land looked better after that trip than it ever had before.
I learned not to stand up just because I spotted something interesting.
The waves found every reason to slap us awake.
I was certain we had drifted off course at least three times.
The worst part was not knowing what moved beneath us.
I would take the boat again, but only with a clearer sky.
You trusted that little hull more than I did.
I can still feel the ground swaying when I think about it.
The first tree on shore looked like an old friend.
I packed for a journey and forgot to pack for being soaked.
Whatever else went wrong, at least the boat brought us home.
Soil remembers boots, rain, and kindness. It is not as quiet as people think.
Good fields are made of patience, fences, and someone awake before the sun.
A good harvest feeds us through the days when nothing grows.
The smell before rain reaches me faster than most village news.
I can tell a dry week by how the ground cracks around the water channel.
Clouds over the western roof usually mean I should cover the seed before supper.
One late frost taught me never to trust the first warm morning.
The field darkens after good rain. That color settles my nerves.
When swallows fly low, I finish the outdoor work early.
A hard wind can empty a seed bag faster than any hungry bird.
I remember seasons by the harvest they spared and the harvest they took.
Warm nights make the wheat move differently when dawn comes.
If the soil clings to my boots, it is too wet to work without harm.
The animals grow restless before thunder reaches the village.
A pale sunrise in winter usually means the cold has more to say.
Rain after planting sounds better than any village bell.
I have watched one cloud save a field and another flatten it.
The best weather is the kind nobody needs to discuss by midday.
Every season leaves a different smell in the empty rows.
I still check the sky before making a promise about tomorrow.
